title: Ideas to improve the CI
body:
Here's a collection of ideas to help us improve our CI. The goal is to make it faster and cheaper to enable fast iteration times for developers:

## Proposed ideas

- [ ] Investigate why Build-package_release takes that long. Do we always need to build with LTO? Even if LTO gives us the best performance. Do we need that performance for the CI? Maybe we could even compare the perf tests against non-LTO builds?
- [ ] Add a new job for [IWYU](https://include-what-you-use.org/) to avoid including unused headers
- [x] Run binary_tidy also for sync PRs
- [ ] Check in StyleCheck only the diff. Does it need to be a block? Can't we decouple it and run it in parallel?
- [ ] [Huge] Rewrite tests using no-parallel to parallelize them
- [ ] [Huge] Improve C++ build times
    - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/74727
    - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/75153
    - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/75141,  

## Done

- [x] Disable merge-commit: [#74600](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/74600)
- [x] Move Integration test flaky to Tests_1 to have early feedback: #74710
- [x] Move binary_tidy and release to an earlier non-blocking stage in parallel to Builds_1 to report static analysis and Tests_1 issues ASAP: #74665
- [x] Run StyleCheck and FastTest in parallel: #74916
- [x] Test mold linker: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/87681
- [x] Test wild linker: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/87674

## Discarded ideas

- Only run tests if only tests are added/modified. Run them 1000 times in parallel
	- Looking for flakiness is already implemented. The `Stateless tests flaky check (asan)` ([50 times in 8 parallel jobs](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/12807735754/job/35709922632#step:8:4424)) and `Integration tests flaky check (asan)` ([3 times where we run 5 times each test, but sequentially](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/12807735754/job/35709922632#step:8:4424)) jobs. There is no flaky check for stateful tests, though. I guess that's because they're the minority. The rest of the jobs are always run even if only 1 test is added/modified. In any case, we can assume that the number of PRs modifying only tests is minimum, so let's focus on some other low-hanging fruit that gives us more energy

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> Add a new job for [IWYU](https://include-what-you-use.org/) to avoid including unused headers

Re IWYU (and https://clang.llvm.org/extra/clang-include-fixer.html): Forget about it. Even with moderately complex codebases, they add _tons_ of includes for missing headers (I remember 100+ includes added per file in some cases). This is overkill and nobody likes to deal with that. The problem (the included headers blow up compile + link times) can be addressed in a simpler manner:
1. _Aggressively move code from headers into source files_. Ask PR authors for this even if it means writing a little bit more code.
2. Do not templatize as much, and as a consequence, move even more code from headers to source files. Templates are used in places where they make zero difference in the scope of the entire database.

Worth a try for sure but I think ClickHouse's includes as a whole are too entangled. Imagine A includes B, A includes C, B includes C. Now remove the include of C from A. As per transitivity, A still includes C (via B). I don't have big hopes here.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
>  Investigate why Build-package_release takes that long

LTO. It easily adds +30 min to linking (in my local builds).

We should ship an LTOed release binary but CI binaries don't necessarily need to have LTO. Omitting LTO in CI would (very likely) not impair the validity of performance tests results. We can assume that green (red) performance tests on a CI build without LTO translate to no (a) performance problem in the release build with LTO.

I remember @participant11 mentioned that some Cloud builds are taken from CI? That would be a problem indeed. Maybe we can remove LTO only in the public CI but keep it in the private repo. Needs clarification.

comments.author: participant1
participant1
comments.body:
> Only run tests if only tests are added/modified. Run them 1000 times in parallel

Hmm. Any PR, no matter what and how much code changes, can mess up any tests, even if the PR does not add/change new/existing tests. In some sense, our CI is one big "flaky" check and it is a good thing, IMHO.

Removing "no-parallel" is more impactful to reduce CI runtimes, I think.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
There are two more things we can do to reduce CI costs.

1. Run no-parallel tests in parallel on two CH instances: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68919
This PR is _almost_ finished, I just need to carefully review the failing tests. As a result, the tests run 27% faster overall, which allows us to reduce the number of job batches and keep the total test execution time to about an hour. But there are some memory issues, instead of 64GB, each instance get ~half of that, and some tests require more memory.

2. Merge stateless and stateful tests jobs into a single functional tests job. 
A full run of the stateful tests job takes 10 minutes, while the tests in this job run for 5 minutes. Removing stateful jobs and runnings them with the stateless tests will save a couple of bucks.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> > Only run tests if only tests are added/modified. Run them 1000 times in parallel
> 
> Hmm. Any PR, no matter what and how much code changes, can mess up any tests, even if the PR does not add/change new/existing tests. In some sense, our CI is one big "flaky" check and it is a good thing, IMHO.
> 
> Removing "no-parallel" is more impactful to reduce CI runtimes, I think.

I completely agree with you. That's why the task says "run tests if only tests are added/modified". The use case is where you fix a flaky tests, for instance. The moment that there's any change in the C++ source code or any flag/dependency we need to run the whole suite.

e.g. of fixing a shell test: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/74648 [triggers the whole test suite](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/12807735754) unnecessarily. Why don't we run only `Stateless tests flaky check (asan)` to check whether that particular test (or any other modified tests) are flaky?

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
> e.g. of fixing a shell test: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/74648 [triggers the whole test suite](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/12807735754) unnecessarily. Why don't we run only Stateless tests flaky check (asan) to check whether that particular test (or any other modified tests) are flaky?

1. How does the CI determine that a modified test should only be run in the "Stateless tests flaky check (asan)" job variant? While the test modification might pass in this variant, it could potentially fail in another variant, such as "Stateless tests (s3)."

2. If we limit the execution to only the modified tests within a job, I’m concerned this might be too strong optimization for our CI. We usemultiple randomized tweaks, such as ClickHouse settings, test-case order, where specific tests may fail only when run alongside others or in a certain sequence or with specific settings. Running the same tests across multiple jobs alongside with other tests provides broader coverage to help identify problems faster.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
>1. How does the CI determine that a modified test should only be run in the "Stateless tests flaky check (asan)" job variant? While the test modification might pass in this variant, it could potentially fail in another variant, such as "Stateless tests (s3)."

That's a good point. The option that makes more sense to me is to run a flaky check for the tests modified for all variants.

>2. If we limit the execution to only the modified tests within a job, I’m concerned this might be too strong optimization for our CI. We usemultiple randomized tweaks, such as ClickHouse settings, test-case order, where specific tests may fail only when run alongside others or in a certain sequence or with specific settings. Running the same tests across multiple jobs alongside with other tests provides broader coverage to help identify problems faster.

Also a good point. We can't run every possible combination in any case.
If we can't run flaky jobs for all flavors (which I think it's a good idea, anyway), I agree we may discard this idea because it'll lead to too many untested scenarios.

Tip from @participant4 to visualize in a flamegraph the CI pipeline:

```sql
SELECT
    if(instance_id == '', (rand()::UInt8)::String, instance_id)  AS group,
    commit_sha,
    check_name AS operation_name,
    toUnixTimestamp(check_start_time)*1000/60 AS start_time_us, -- it will be in minutes, I think
    toUnixTimestamp(check_start_time + toIntervalMillisecond(check_duration_ms))*1000/60 AS finish_time_us,
    sipHash64(operation_name) AS color,
    map('url', report_url) AS attribute
FROM checks
WHERE 1 AND (test_name = '') AND (report_url != '') AND (commit_sha = '310f00ec8bd734d6d1c05b317707b627cc3f28db')
ORDER BY
    check_start_time ASC,
    start_time_us ASC INTO OUTFILE '/Users/<user>/Downloads/310f00ec8bd734d6d1c05b317707b627cc3f28db.json' TRUNCATE
FORMAT JSON
SETTINGS output_format_json_named_tuples_as_objects = 1
```

However, looking at some random run of stateful tests in CI I found ([here](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/74070/d46f8833f7ce5d96d697cb3d9fbe47a7448eb4ab/stateful_tests__aarch64__asan_.html)), their runtimes are not excessive at all. comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
> Yes, this may increase job runtime. However, looking at some random run of stateful tests in CI I found ([here](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/74070/d46f8833f7ce5d96d697cb3d9fbe47a7448eb4ab/stateful_tests__aarch64__asan_.html)), their runtimes are not excessive at all. To clarify: Do they run on significantly more powerful VMs than stateless tests?

Stateful tests run on the same VM types as Stateless tests. They run quick due to limited number of test cases, none of which are particularly long-running. Stateless tests, however, are slow primarily due to long-runnning **non-parallel** test cases: ~600 test cases take ~45 minutes to run. In contrast, ~6000 **parallel** test cases take just 10 minutes of runtime. Thus, more than 75% of compute time for stateless tests are underutilised (non-parallel test run), adding stateful test cases making them non-parallel exacerbates this issue.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:

The bigger problem seem the existing 600 non-parallel tests ... which is largely technical debt which we either need to address by
- removing these tags (see e.g. #67914),
- @participant2's #68919,
- or somehow move them out of regular tests for PRs (e.g. run them 1x nightly instead which has its own disadvantages).

comments.author: participant6
comments.body:
Today while looking at reports I was reminded again how slow release build times are due to link times. Some ideas:
* Give mold another try. It's come a long way since I last tested it and it supports LTO.
* Try using LLD incremental LTO with cache (and keep the cache in CI). It might be really useful in small PRs. We could consider enabling LTO cache in the proejct by default.
* We are linking multiple executable files ([example](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/PRs/75730/4422f67298b84505019f5fb75c74b35ea4f37b5b//build_amd_release/build_log.log) look for `Linking CXX executable`) . Some small and insignificant but some aren't. Do we really need `clickhouse-odbc-bridge`, `clickhouse-library-bridge`, or `clickhouse-keeper` LTO builds in all PRs? Can't we just build clickhouse main binary instead? We could keep the other binaries in master builds if we need them.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
[A question about why the tidy job took so long](https://<redacted-host>/archives/C02N5V7EU57/p1749135404983869?thread_ts=1741796223.775679&cid=C02N5V7EU57) made me take a look to see whether there was an easy way to detect how many dependencies each of the translation units (TUs) have. This is a complement to the current [build_trace_log metrics we collect in our CI to know in which files most time is spent](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/74727#issuecomment-2601867906).

That allows us to know which header files are included in most places and also how many TUs require to be recompiled after changes in specific header files.

The idea is to ask ninja to generate a dependency file, parse it, ingest it into ClickHouse and then analyze there. The format is quite straightforward:

```bash
ninja -C build -t deps > deps.txt
head deps.txt

contrib/libunwind-cmake/CMakeFiles/unwind.dir/__/llvm-project/libunwind/src/Unwind-EHABI.cpp.o: #deps 3, deps mtime 1749051560090791134 (VALID)
    ../contrib/llvm-project/libunwind/src/Unwind-EHABI.cpp
    ../contrib/llvm-project/libunwind/src/Unwind-EHABI.h
    ../contrib/llvm-project/libunwind/include/__libunwind_config.h

contrib/libunwind-cmake/CMakeFiles/unwind.dir/__/llvm-project/libunwind/src/UnwindRegistersRestore.S.o: #deps 2, deps mtime 1749051560086791103 (VALID)
    /home/<user>/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/contrib/llvm-project/libunwind/src/UnwindRegistersRestore.S
    /home/<user>/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/contrib/llvm-project/libunwind/src/assembly.h
```

I wrote a simple script to parse that file and ingest it into a `build_deps` table: https://pastila.nl/?002b8225/3d0f9c5ff11823ae2b9f76d572580a92#1TdQSWE5Vbo686FPtJ566A==

And now we can query things such as which header is included the most:

```sql
SELECT
    dependency,
    count()
FROM build_deps
WHERE dependency ILIKE '%src%'
GROUP BY dependency
ORDER BY 2 DESC
LIMIT 20

Query id: abef8c91-d941-4631-9556-ca35caccf98a

    ┌─dependency──────────────────────────────────┬─count()─┐
 1. │ ../src/Common/Logger.h                      │    3357 │
 2. │ ../src/Common/LoggingFormatStringHelpers.h  │    3353 │
 3. │ ../src/Core/LogsLevel.h                     │    3353 │
 4. │ ../src/Common/Exception.h                   │    3351 │
 5. │ ../src/Common/StackTrace.h                  │    3351 │
 6. │ ../src/Core/Defines.h                       │    3181 │
 7. │ ../src/Core/Types_fwd.h                     │    3047 │
 8. │ ../src/Core/TypeId.h                        │    3001 │
 9. │ ../src/Core/Types.h                         │    2981 │
10. │ ../src/Interpreters/Context_fwd.h           │    2948 │
11. │ ../src/Core/Names.h                         │    2915 │
12. │ ../src/Common/Allocator_fwd.h               │    2757 │
13. │ ../src/Common/Allocator.h                   │    2740 │
14. │ ../src/Common/AllocationTrace.h             │    2735 │
15. │ ../src/Common/typeid_cast.h                 │    2638 │
16. │ ../src/Common/CurrentMemoryTracker.h        │    2633 │
```

comments.author: participant9
comments.body:
It is possible to implement configurable workflows on Github. I think adding an option for a trusted user to run a specific test (maybe a stress test) via configurable github workflow for a specific branch is easy to implement and this will help those who may have problems running `praktika` locally due to memory or performance constraints of their own hardware.

I believe this is another idea that is worth documenting at least. 1. Create and cache a C++ coverage report for each test. 2. Run the relevant functional tests if the coverage report matches changes made by a developer (i.e. if they both target the same functional unit). 3. This also allows reminding the developer that if they commit code with no test coverage, it is a good idea to add a test for the change. This helps to quickly identify problems with new functionality and cancel the entire run saving both resources and developers' time.

Hey @reporter,

I've just stumbled on this myself. It seems that despite both lld and mold using multi processing for linking, both of them are stuck for about an hour utilizing only one core. I tried to use lld's incremental linking, but it only reduced the linking time from 1h10min to about 1h. You can analyze the linking process adding a `--time-trace` to `lld`:

```diff
diff --git a/CMakeLists.txt b/CMakeLists.txt
index 2334779289b..e3adca47bec 100644
--- a/CMakeLists.txt
+++ b/CMakeLists.txt
@@ -361,7 +361,8 @@ if (ENABLE_THINLTO AND NOT ENABLE_TESTS AND NOT SANITIZE)
     # Link time optimization
     set (CMAKE_C_FLAGS_RELWITHDEBINFO "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS_RELWITHDEBINFO} -flto=thin -fwhole-program-vtables")
     set (CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELWITHDEBINFO "${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELWITHDEBINFO} -flto=thin -fwhole-program-vtables")
-    set (CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS_RELWITHDEBINFO "${CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS_RELWITHDEBINFO} -flto=thin -fwhole-program-vtables")
+    set (CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS_RELWITHDEBINFO "${CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS_RELWITHDEBINFO} -flto=thin -fwhole-program-vtables -Wl,--time-trace")
 elseif (ENABLE_THINLTO)
     message (${RECONFIGURE_MESSAGE_LEVEL} "Cannot enable ThinLTO")
 endif ()
```

Then, you'll get a `clickhouse.time-trace` file next to `clickhouse` binary. You can open this file in `chrome://tracing` (on Chromium browsers), but it wasn't necessarily obvious for me what's the exact reason for this even with this file. I can see that `lld` has spent 56 minutes on `OptModule`, but I didn't dig further to see if that's something that could be optimized.

comments.body:
@participant10 thanks for the tip! Presumably we could just enable `ENABLE_BUILD_PROFILING=1` (which we do for CI builds) to get the same result as per https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/e864c7257d92882ab189bd76fc6e0e507d651261/CMakeLists.txt#L281-L284

We're not storing the trace as artifacts, though. But we're injecting them into a private ClickHouse server. I'll check to see if I can find anything interesting there 👍 

> but it wasn't necessarily obvious for me what's the exact reason for this even with this file. I can see that `lld` has spent 56 minutes on `OptModule`, but I didn't dig further to see if that's something that could be optimized.

My understanding here of ThinLTO is that the linker is in charge of identifying which parts should be optimized as separate modules (as opposed to "fat" LTO which puts everything altogether, but it's not an option for a huge project like ClickHouse because of the memory it'd consume AFAIK). This should be a quick thing for the linker. Now, the linker should exec the compiler to generate the native code for each of the modules. This is where the bottleneck is supposed to be. Maybe the trace provided by lld is a single black box in which it doesn't differentiate each of the different compiler calls. I'll try to check and investigate. I guess we could also wrap those compiler calls to see where times are spent per module.
